text.p: Though they both officially deny it, North Korea and the United States appear to be using food as a weapon in peace talks, leaving the communist nation's starving people as the helpless victims in a political game.

One Japanese analyst likened the issue to a game of "chicken" to see who blinked first -- North Korea in insisting that major food supplies precede peace talks, or the United States in holding out for negotiations first.
So did North Korea half-blink this weekend when it said its soldiers would symbolically turn their swords into ploughshares by taking on any agricultural task in the coming months?
Shinya Kato, an analyst at Radio Press, a Tokyo-based agency which monitors North Korea's official media, thinks so.
"North Korea definitely needs the food so it can't be too stubborn. I think North Korea will eventually compromise," he told Reuters on Monday.

In a broadcast on Sunday, official North Korean Radio said the country's soldiers "must further solidify the unity of the army and people and achieve a bumper harvest this year without fail by launching into the struggle to assist rural areas and actively contribute to agricultural production".
It said soldiers would take "a plunge into water or fire for any task to increase grain output for the people".
The coming months until a new harvest begins in September are regarded as key to averting a catastrophic famine among North Korea's 23 million people.

The announcement on the military was regarded as a veiled answer to some Western nations' reluctance to give aid to a nation which has managed to keep its 1.1 million troops under arms, despite its economic plight.
Western diplomatic reports in recent weeks of full scale military training exercises in North Korea, the biggest for two years, had appeared to coincide with a sudden caution about giving aid.
Devastated by floods in 1995 and 1996, North Korea needs at least 1.3 million tonnes of additional food to meet just its basic needs this year, a United Nations food aid agency said recently.
The United States, which strongly denies any suggestion of using food aid as a weapon to get North Korea to the negotiating table, has been in the forefront of pledging "humanitarian aid".

But it has firmly held out against North Korean hints that a major aid package of not just food would persuade Pyongyang's rulers to consider starting talks also involving China and South Korea to formally close the book on the 1950-53 Korean war which ended in an armistice.
At the same time, the United States has sent out its own signals that once peace talks start, stepped up aid is a strong possibility.
Even as reports grow of the dire situation in North Korea, doubts still persist about how close North Korea is to a Somalia or Ethiopia-type disaster.

"The big question is how serious the food situation is. They are obviously short of food, but at least the North Korean official media we monitor does not give an impression that they are extremely desperate for food," Radiopress' Kato said.
"We can't tell whether North Korea is purposely exaggerating the food situation or whether they really are desperate," he added.
"In any case the turning point will likely come in the next few months."
